title: Class 11 Relations and Functions: The Complete CBSE Guide (with Quiz)
meta_title: Class 11 Relations and Functions: CBSE Guide + Quiz
meta_desc: Master Class 11 Relations and Functions (CBSE): Cartesian product, domain and range, function types and real functions, plus a free 8-question quiz.
excerpt: Most students lose marks in this chapter not on the hard problems but on the definitions: what exactly is the difference between a relation and a function, or between range and codomain? Here is the whole Class 11 chapter, sorted out, with an 8-question quiz at the end.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Relations and Functions sits early in the Class 11 CBSE syllabus, and that placement fools a lot of students into treating it as easy revision from Class 10. It is not. This is the chapter where the language of the whole subject gets defined — ordered pairs, Cartesian product, domain, range, mappings — and if the definitions stay fuzzy here, everything from limits to calculus in Class 12 feels harder than it should. Get this chapter genuinely solid and you have bought yourself two years of easier maths.

What follows is the entire chapter in the order the NCERT textbook builds it, with the exact points examiners test and the mistakes I see students make year after year.

Ordered pairs and the Cartesian product

An ordered pair (a, b) is just two elements written in a fixed order. The order matters: (2, 3) and (3, 2) are different pairs. That single idea is the foundation of the whole chapter, so do not wave past it.

The Cartesian product of two sets A and B, written A × B, is the set of all ordered pairs where the first element comes from A and the second from B. If A = {1, 2} and B = {x, y}, then A × B = {(1, x), (1, y), (2, x), (2, y)}. Notice the count: if A has m elements and B has n elements, A × B has exactly m × n pairs. That n(A × B) = n(A) × n(B) result shows up in almost every exam as a one-mark question, so bank it.

A quick warning: A × B is not the same as B × A unless the sets are equal. Students lose easy marks by treating the product as if order does not matter.

What a relation actually is

A relation R from set A to set B is simply a subset of A × B. That is the whole definition. Any collection of ordered pairs drawn from the Cartesian product is a relation — it does not need a nice formula, though it usually has one, like R = {(x, y) : y = x + 1}.

Three words get tested constantly, so pin them down now:

  • Domain — the set of all first elements of the ordered pairs in R.
  • Range — the set of all second elements that actually appear in R.
  • Codomain — the whole set B, whether or not every element of it gets used.

The range is always a subset of the codomain, and it can be smaller. Confusing the two is probably the single most common error in this chapter. If A has m elements and B has n elements, the number of possible relations from A to B is 2 raised to the power (m × n), because a relation is any subset of the m × n pairs.

Functions: the special relations

A function f from A to B is a relation in which every element of A is paired with exactly one element of B. Two conditions, both compulsory: no element of the domain is left out, and none is paired with two different outputs.

The vertical line test is the visual version. Draw the graph; if any vertical line cuts it more than once, it is not a function. A circle fails, a parabola opening upward passes.

Types of functions you must recognise

TypeConditionPlain-English meaning
One-one (injective)Different inputs give different outputsNo two x-values share a y-value
Onto (surjective)Range equals codomainEvery element of B is hit
IntoRange is a proper subset of codomainSome element of B is never hit
Many-oneTwo or more inputs share an outputThe opposite of one-one

Class 11 introduces these ideas; the formal proofs of one-one and onto get heavier in Class 12, but examiners here already ask you to classify simple functions, so learn to spot them.

Real functions and their domain and range

A real function takes real numbers to real numbers. The exam's favourite question is finding the domain — the set of x-values for which the formula is actually defined. Two rules cover most cases:

  • You cannot divide by zero, so any x that makes a denominator zero is excluded.
  • Under a square root you need a non-negative number, so set the expression inside ≥ 0 and solve.

For example, the domain of f(x) = 1/(x − 3) is all real numbers except 3. The domain of f(x) = √(x − 2) is x ≥ 2. Finding the range is often trickier — you reason about what outputs the formula can produce. For f(x) = x², the range is all non-negative reals, because a square is never negative.

The standard functions to know cold

NCERT lists a handful of real functions with fixed domains and ranges that examiners assume you know: the identity function f(x) = x, constant functions, the modulus function f(x) = |x|, the signum function, the greatest integer function [x], and simple polynomial and rational functions. Learn the shape and the domain-range of each — a graph question on the modulus or greatest-integer function is close to guaranteed.

Common CBSE problem types and where marks leak

Across board papers and school exams, the recurring questions are: computing n(A × B) or listing the product; finding A and B from a given product; stating domain, range and codomain of a relation; testing whether a relation is a function; and finding the domain or range of a real function. The predictable mark-losers are equally consistent — treating range and codomain as the same, forgetting that a function must map every input, and missing an excluded value in a domain because a denominator quietly hits zero.

One honest piece of advice: do not just memorise the definitions, write them out in your own words and then test them against odd examples. Ask yourself whether R = {(1, 2), (1, 3)} is a function (it is not — input 1 has two outputs). That habit of stress-testing a definition is what separates the students who score 6 out of 6 on this chapter from the ones who lose two marks to a careless slip.

Practise before the exam

Below is a free 8-question quiz built exactly on this chapter — Cartesian products, domain and range, and function types — pitched at Class 11 level. Try it, then read the explanations for anything you miss. When you want longer, exam-style practice with full solutions, the case-study workbook linked at the end walks through the CBSE question patterns step by step.

quiz.title: Class 11 Relations and Functions Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight questions on Cartesian products, relations, domain and range, and types of functions. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.

questions.q: If A = {1, 2, 3} and B = {a, b}, how many elements does A × B have?
A relation R from A to B is best described as:
options: A function from A to B
questions.explanation: By definition a relation from A to B is any subset of the Cartesian product A × B.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT a function?
questions.explanation: In {(1, 2), (1, 3), ...} the input 1 is paired with two different outputs, so it fails the one-output rule for a function.

questions.q: The set of all second elements that actually appear in a relation is its:
questions.explanation: The range is the set of second elements that appear; the codomain is the whole target set B, which may be larger.

questions.q: What is the domain of f(x) = 1/(x − 4)?
questions.explanation: The denominator is zero when x = 4, so x = 4 is excluded. The domain is all reals except 4.

questions.q: What is the domain of f(x) = √(x − 5)?
questions.explanation: The expression under the root must be ≥ 0, so x − 5 ≥ 0, giving x ≥ 5.

questions.q: A function in which different inputs always give different outputs is called:
questions.explanation: A one-one (injective) function maps distinct inputs to distinct outputs. Many-one is the opposite.

questions.q: For a function f: A → B, if the range equals the codomain B, the function is:
questions.explanation: When the range equals the codomain — every element of B is hit — the function is onto (surjective).

faq.q: What is the difference between a relation and a function in Class 11?
faq.a: A relation from A to B is any set of ordered pairs from A × B. A function is a special relation in which every element of A is paired with exactly one element of B — no input left out, and no input with two outputs. Every function is a relation, but not every relation is a function.

faq.q: What is the difference between range and codomain?
faq.a: The codomain is the entire target set B that you declare when defining the function. The range is only the part of B that is actually produced as an output. The range is always a subset of the codomain and can be smaller — confusing the two is the most common mistake in this chapter.

faq.q: How do I find the domain of a real function?
faq.a: Look for values of x that break the formula. Exclude any x that makes a denominator zero, and for a square root require the expression inside to be greater than or equal to zero, then solve that inequality. Whatever real numbers survive both checks form the domain.

faq.q: Is Relations and Functions an important chapter for exams?
faq.a: Yes. It carries direct one- and two-mark questions in Class 11 exams (Cartesian product counts, domain and range, function testing), and it is the foundation for the Class 12 chapter on inverse and composite functions. A weak grasp here quietly costs marks in calculus later.
